div.p: With friendly greetings from us all. I wrote to WBY thanking and declining. Who are the committee he speaks of and are you accepting?

div.note: The postmark on this postcard seems to show “18” for the day, and “24” for the year. JJ wrote to Jane Heap from Saint-Malo on 16 July 1924, and to Sylvia Beach on 17 July from the same location. On 21 July, still in Saint-Malo, he wrote to Fritz Vanderpyl. We thus infer the month of July.

The face of the postcard shows a tinted photograph of horse-drawn carriages, drivers, and pedestrians before a large double gateway, with the caption “Saint-Malo – La Porte Chateaubriand – The Chateaubriand Gateway – LL.” François-René, vicomte de Chateaubriand (1768–1848), French writer, politician, and historian, was born in Saint-Malo and, at his request, was buried there. The postcard was produced by Lévy et Neurdein Réunis, a French printing house and photograph publishing company in Paris, founded around 1920.

Partly to rest from recent eye surgery, JJ took his family to Saint-Malo, a French port in Brittany on the English Channel, arriving about 7 July and staying until mid-August at the Grand Hôtel de France et Chateaubriand. Here he listened to the Latin-laced Breton language and compared it to Irish, observed a noisy fair in progress under his hotel windows, and attempted to work on parts of “Work in Progress,” later to be published as Finnegans Wake (1939) (Ellmann, JJ 566-67). JJ’s hotel overlooked the sea and the ramparts of the old town with their wide promenade along the top. The accommodations were described in a contemporary guidebook as “Comfortable family hotel; modern comfort; all rooms with hot and cold water and central heating. Pension, frs. 30-35” (Bradshaw’s Continental Guide, pt. 2 [London: Henry Blacklock & Co., 1924], 46). An earlier reviewer had opined, more ambivalently, that the hotel, “the ancient home of the author [Chateaubriand] himself – is very good indeed, but a typical tourist hotel where one eats at one of those interminable long drawn-out tables d’hôte, the curse of all resort hotels” (Francis Miltoun, “A Little Tour in Brittany,” The Automobile, vol. 16, no. 25 [20 June 1907], 1010).

note.p: The Irish poet and dramatist W.B. Yeats (1865-1939) had become a senator of the newly established Irish Free State, following the Anglo-Irish Treaty of December 1921 that ended the Irish war of independence against Britain. The new Irish government created the Tailteann Games (Aonach Tailteann) as a sporting and cultural festival to be hosted in 1924. In addition to athletic events, chess, golf, boating competitions, and artistic exhibitions, there was a cultural program that awarded prizes through the Royal Irish Academy. Irish recipients of literary prizes in 1924 were Stephen MacKenna, Oliver St. John Gogarty, Francis Stuart, and James Stephens.

Yeats wrote JJ from Dublin on 1 July 1924, care of Pound, to invite him to “come and stay with us for the Horse Show and the Tailteann Games some time between August 1st and August 10th, or for that period.” Yeats had urged the Tailteann Distinguished Visitors’ Committee “to send you an official invitation to come as the guest of the Nation. I do not expect, however, to succeed. I can imagine the horror with which the suggestion will be received by, for instance, the Marquis McSwiney [sic], Chamberlain to the Pope.” In a postscript dated 5 July Yeats added: “Yes the Committee did all but unanimously decide not to send you an official invitation” (The Collected Letters of W.B. Yeats, Electronic Edition, Unpublished Letters [1905-1939]).

Technically, JJ was deemed ineligible for a literary prize because he was not resident in Ireland. Writing to Harriet Shaw Weaver, he expressed “great satisfaction” in receiving Yeats’s letter, copies of which he was having made (LIII 100). But he wrote Yeats on 12 July to decline the personal invitation, pleading his recent eye surgery and thanking him “for the expression of friendly admiration with which you have honoured me” (LIII 100). In awarding the literary prizes, Yeats observed: “We feel … that it is our duty to say that Mr. James Joyce’s book [Ulysses], though as obscene as Rabelais, and therefore forbidden by law in England and the United States, is more indubitably a work of genius than any prose written by an Irishman since the death of Synge” (quoted in Ellmann, JJ 566-67 n.‡). Finnegans Wake makes mention of “the tailturn horseshow” (FW 386).

div.note: The literary prize committee for the 1924 Tailteann Games consisted of the Irish writers W.B. Yeats, as chairman; George Russell (“AE”) (1867-1935); and Lennox Robinson (1886-1958) (“News Notes,” Poetry, vol. 25, no. 2 [November 1924]: 114). The Distinguished Visitors’ Committee, which issued invitations for the Games, included Yeats as chairman; Oliver St. John Gogarty (1878-1957), vice-chairman; Sir Henry McLaughlin (1876-1927); Sir Simon Maddock (1869-1927); and the Marquis MacSwiney (1871-1945) (R.F. Foster, W.B. Yeats: A Life. II. The Arch-Poet 1915-1939 [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2003], 713 n.30).

note.p: On 17 June 1924, Yeats wrote Pound from Dublin “to come and stay with us for the Tailteann Games and the Horse Show. You will be nominally the guest of the Nation and I enclose you a very magnificent invitation card. … I shall have a small Committee acting with me, selected by myself and you will hear Joyce sufficiently commented I hope, though certainly not crowned, for he is excluded by the terms of reference. You will also probably be invited to certain country houses, and will be generally made much of, and meet everybody who is to be met, and have admirable opportunities for your usual violence and brutality” (The Collected Letters of W.B. Yeats, Electronic Edition, Unpublished Letters [1905-1939]). The enclosed invitation, signed by Yeats as chairman, read: “We, on behalf of the / Distinguished Visitors’ Committee of / Aonach Tailteann / have the honour to invite you, / Ezra Pound Esqre M.A. / an Eminent Son of your Country, / to be the Guest of our Nation, / from 1st August to 10th August, 1924.” Pound wrote his father on 21 June: “The OIRISH, bedad, have sent me a foot square of paste board calling me an Emmynent son av my counthry (we suppose its intended as a compliment) [and inviting] me to be a guest bedad of their Nation; during the national barbaric games and horse show (in gaelic).” He added, “The naygotiations are pending” (Ezra Pound to His Parents: Letters 1895-1929, ed. Mary de Rachewiltz et al. [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010], 534). The negotiations concerned two of Pound’s particular detestations, censorship and passport regulations, both of which he considered to be illegitimate restrictions on the ability of minds and bodies to travel over borders freely. He wanted an assurance from Yeats that Ireland was “a separate enough state to have an open port” that would admit Ulysses, unlike Britain where copies were being seized at customs. He also wanted to be “exempt from passport imbecilities” and to avoid English ports and their “damn emigration formalities.” If these were not deal-breakers enough, he also wondered if Yeats could arrange a concert of the music of the American avant-garde composer George Antheil (1900-1959), or a performance of Pound’s own opera for voices and small orchestra, Le Testament de Villon (1923), perhaps to be staged at the Abbey Theatre in Dublin (see “Letters to William Butler Yeats,” ed. C.F. Terrell, Antæus, whole no. 21/22 [Spring/Summer 1976]: 34-49).

Hard pressed to meet such terms, Yeats wrote Pound on 26 June 1924 that, while English obscenity law applied in Ireland, “[n]o such prosecution [of Ulysses] has taken place hitherto and ‘The Irish bookshop’ sell copies of the books & puts it in the Window” (The Collected Letters of W.B. Yeats, Electronic Edition, Unpublished Letters [1905-1939]). As for avoiding English ports, Yeats advised: “Come by long sea from Havre & [Desmond] Fitzgerald [Minister for External Affairs] says you will have no trouble of any kind about pass-port” (ibid.). These “naygotiations” produced a lively postal exchange, but Pound did not go to Ireland for the Tailteann Games.

Literary awards were much in the air and much on Pound’s mind at this time. Yeats had received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923 “for his always inspired poetry, which in a highly artistic form gives expression to the spirit of a whole nation,” as the Swedish Academy’s citation read. On the evening after he received the news, Yeats gave a dinner party at the Shelbourne Hotel in Dublin. “During dinner the first telegram of congratulation arrived. It was (to [Yeats’s] immense gratification) from James Joyce” (Joseph Hone, W.B. Yeats, 1865-1939 [London: Macmillan, 1967], 356). Yeats, the first Irish recipient of the Nobel Literature Prize, went to Stockholm in December 1923 to receive the medal on behalf of himself and his nation. The prize came with £7,500.

Pound believed, rather unrealistically, that “if the award had not gone to Mr Yeats it should have been given to his most distinguished compatriot, the author of ‘ULYSSES’ … and if it can not, for some national reason, go for two consecutive years to the same nation; one might nominate James Joyce as representative of the republic of letters, or of the Heimatlos [homeless, displaced]; who are, at this moment as respectable a collection of writers as is found in any one country” (“Le Prix Nobel,” Der Querschnitt, vol. 4, no. 1 [Spring 1924]: 41, 43). Shortly after the publication of Ulysses, Desmond Fitzgerald (1888-1947), then Minister of Publicity in the Irish Free State government, visited JJ in Paris and said that he was thinking of urging his cabinet to nominate him for the Nobel Prize. JJ wrote his brother: “He will probably lose his portfolio without obtaining the prize for me” (LIII 61). Neither JJ nor Pound would ever be a recipient of what Yeats called “the bounty of Sweden.”
